outline.chapter_title: From Violent Night to Federal Firearm Case
outline.description: This chapter sets out the factual and procedural foundation of the case: the November 2020 incident at D.F.’s home, the police response and later standoff, the discovery of the sawed-off rifle, the federal felon-in-possession charge, the Armed Career Criminal Act finding, and the issues Cutbank raised on appeal. It gives students the factual map needed to understand why the evidentiary disputes and sentencing enhancement mattered.
subtopics: The events inside D.F.’s home: methamphetamine use, threats, confinement in a closet, and striking D.F. with the gun
Other witnesses in the house, including D.F.’s sons and housemate C.F., and why their presence mattered
Cutbank’s flight from the home with D.F.’s phone and the firearm
The second police call: Cutbank barricading himself in a nearby garage and making erratic statements
Resistance to arrest, including biting an officer and grabbing for the officer’s gun
Physical evidence recovered along the likely path of flight: D.F.’s phone, a knife, and the sawed-off Marlin .22 rifle
DNA evidence and witness identification linking Cutbank to the rifle
The federal charge under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) and the enhanced penalty framework of 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)
The jury’s conviction on the possession charge and its finding of at least three prior violent felony convictions
The district court’s sentence of 292 months and the basic structure of the advisory Guidelines calculation
The issues on appeal: multiple evidentiary and procedural objections plus a challenge to the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement
The appellate court’s framing of the appeal as a series of largely unsupported claims

outline.chapter_title: Pretrial Evidentiary Rulings: Prior Sightings of the Rifle, Hearsay Concerns, and the Confrontation Clause
outline.description: This chapter explains the court’s treatment of the two main pretrial evidentiary disputes. First, it analyzes why testimony that D.F. and C.F. had previously seen Cutbank with the same rifle was treated as intrinsic proof of possession rather than impermissible Rule 404(b) propensity evidence. Second, it shows why the district court did not abuse its discretion by refusing Cutbank’s requested instruction limiting the jury’s use of D.F.’s statements to police before she testified.
subtopics: Cutbank’s motion in limine to exclude testimony that D.F. and C.F. had seen him with the rifle before the charged incident
The difference between intrinsic evidence and Rule 404(b) evidence
Why prior possession of the same firearm can help prove later possession by showing ownership or control
The Eighth Circuit’s reliance on United States v. Battle for the continuous-possession rationale
How D.F.’s and C.F.’s prior-sighting testimony fit the government’s theory of the case
Cutbank’s request for a jury instruction restricting use of D.F.’s out-of-court statements until she testified
The government’s argument that officers would testify to explain context and police conduct rather than for hearsay purposes
The standard of review for refusing a limiting instruction: abuse of discretion
Why a district court may give a closing instruction instead of an immediate instruction for each item of evidence
The court’s conclusion that the record did not show admission of hearsay requiring the requested protection
Why the Confrontation Clause problem disappeared once D.F. testified in court and was subject to examination
How this chapter’s rulings supported the government’s basic proof that Cutbank knowingly possessed the rifle

outline.chapter_title: At Trial: Renewed Objections, Explanatory Testimony, Impeachment Limits, and Harmless Error
outline.description: This chapter follows the evidentiary disputes that arose during trial itself. It covers the renewed objections to prior-sighting testimony, D.F.’s explanation that she was uncomfortable with guns because her sister had been killed by one, the defense attempt to use a police report to impeach C.F., and the appellate court’s conclusion that none of these rulings—individually or cumulatively—justified reversal.
subtopics: The renewed objection when D.F. testified she had seen the sawed-off rifle a 'handful of times' before the charged night
The related objection to C.F.’s testimony that she had seen the gun 'once or twice' before
Why the appellate court treated these trial objections as controlled by the same intrinsic-evidence ruling made pretrial
Cross-examination of D.F. on prior inconsistent statements about whether she remembered seeing the gun
D.F.’s explanation that she was unfamiliar with and disliked guns because her sister had been killed by one
The motion to strike that testimony and the court’s Rule 403 reasoning that no unfair prejudice or confusion was apparent
The significance of C.F. later mentioning the same fact without a defense objection
The defense effort to undermine C.F. with prior statements to a police investigator
Why the district court allowed questioning about what C.F. said but barred counsel from reading the police report itself without foundation
Authentication requirements for extrinsic impeachment by prior inconsistent statement under United States v. Cumbie
The appellate court’s rebuke to the government for expanding the issues on appeal beyond what Cutbank actually briefed
The harmless-error rule for evidentiary mistakes: reversal only if the jury may have been substantially swayed
The cumulative-error standard and why substantial testimonial and physical evidence defeated any claim of prejudice
What this part of the opinion teaches about broad trial-court discretion over evidence and impeachment

outline.chapter_title: Sentencing: ACCA Status, the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Enhancement, and Appellate Review of a Within-Guidelines Sentence
outline.description: This chapter explains the sentencing analysis in detail. It reconstructs the Guidelines calculation, focuses on the challenged four-level enhancement for possessing the firearm in connection with another felony offense, and distinguishes between procedural correctness in calculating the range and substantive reasonableness in choosing a sentence within that range.
subtopics: The Presentence Investigation Report’s offense-level calculation: base level, altered or obliterated serial number, reckless endangerment during flight, and connection to another felony
Why the sawed-off rifle mattered under 26 U.S.C. § 5845(a)
The jury’s Armed Career Criminal Act finding and its relationship to the Armed Career Criminal guideline in USSG § 4B1.4
The guideline rule that the greater offense level controls
The content of USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B): possession or use of a firearm in connection with another felony offense
Application Note 14(C) and why a separate charge or conviction for the other felony is unnecessary
The district court’s adoption of the PSR’s factual statements without objection and the importance of that procedural fact on appeal
Why the Eighth Circuit found no error, let alone clear error, in concluding that the firearm was used in connection with another felony
Cutbank’s real argument on appeal: not factual insufficiency, but the claim that the enhancement produced a sentence greater than necessary under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)
The sequence required by Gall and Rosales-Mireles: first correctly calculate the Guidelines range, then consider departures or variances under § 3553(a)
The presumption of reasonableness for a within-Guidelines sentence on appeal
How the sentencing record showed the district court reviewed the PSR, the parties’ memoranda, and the § 3553(a) factors
The Eighth Circuit’s inference that the district court considered and rejected Cutbank’s mitigation arguments even without a mechanical recitation
The aggravating facts supporting the 292-month sentence: extensive violent felony history, firearms-related conduct, domestic abuse, kidnapping-like restraint, assault, and injury to an officer
The final holding that the district court neither procedurally erred nor imposed a substantively unreasonable sentence
The case’s broader significance as an illustration of how evidentiary discretion, undeveloped appellate briefing, and deferential sentencing review can combine to produce affirmance
